::: {.why}
The last stylized fact of the week and the one with the most direct consequence for position sizing, because a diversification benefit that disappears in a drawdown was never a diversification benefit.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Report your average pairwise correlation in the calmest and the most volatile deciles of the sample, and say how much diversification is lost between them.
- Say why part of the measured rise is an artifact of conditioning on volatility, and how you would separate the artifact from the real effect.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Quantify last night's plot: bucket the sample by SPY realised volatility decile and report the average pairwise correlation in each. Then translate it into what it costs you, by computing the volatility of an equal-weighted 50-name portfolio implied by each bucket's correlation.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Separate the artifact: simulate 50 series with constant true correlation and time-varying common volatility, then run the same bucketing on the simulation. Some of the effect appears with no change in the true correlation at all, and knowing how much is the difference between a finding and a mistake.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Laloux, Cizeau, Bouchaud & Potters (1998) — Noise Dressing of Financial Correlation Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9810255) [paper]{.res-kind}
